subject: Private namespace cert orchestration and TLS proxying options
messages:
From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@healthtech.io>
To: connor_obrien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
Cc: Infra Team <infra@healthtech.io>
Date: 2026-08-29T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private deployment TLS — where to terminate certs?

Connor,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. We’re moving toward a private VPC deployment for our Redwood runtime and need to finalize how TLS will be handled for private endpoints. Key constraints from our side: PHI data rules, our security team wants Redwood to avoid terminating TLS in a shared public tier, and we need a rotation/incident process that maps to our audit logs.

Questions we need to lock down:
- Do you support TLS passthrough to our LB (so we keep termination inside our VPC)?
- If Redwood terminates, can you support customer-provided certs and integrate with our KMS (we use AWS KMS)?
- How does certificate rotation work (role separation, audit trail, automation)?

I attached a rough SOW and a diagram of our VPC (healthtech_sow.pdf, tls_private_network_diagram.png). Can you outline 2–3 options with tradeoffs (security, operations, testing) and a recommended path for PHI workloads?

Appreciate a quick summary before our compliance review on 09/06.

—Alex
Alex Johnson
Head of Infrastructure, HealthTech Inc
From: connor_obrien <connor.obrien@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@healthtech.io>
Cc: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-08-30T11:35:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Private deployment TLS — where to terminate certs?

Alex — thanks for the context and diagrams, they help. Below are three implementable patterns we commonly use for private deployments, with pros/cons and a recommended approach for PHI. I’ll also call out the minimal network/DNS steps so your infra team can assess effort.

Option A — TLS passthrough to customer LB (no termination in Redwood):
- Flow: Client -> Customer LB (terminates TLS) -> internal connection to Redwood private endpoint (mutual auth optional)
- Pros: Your org retains full control of certs and private key material; easiest for compliance reviews; zero plaintext in public/shared layers.
- Cons: Limits some Redwood platform features (streaming debug headers, early routing at edge); health checks require additional tooling.
- Ops: Customer must ensure LB routes to Redwood private endpoint IPs/FQDNs and handle cert rotation.

Option B — Terminate at Redwood private edge and mTLS to runtime backplanes:
- Flow: Client -> Redwood private endpoint (TLS terminates on customer-dedicated private edge) -> mTLS to Redwood runtime
- Pros: We can perform graceful fallback, do transparent cert rotation on our side, and preserve observability (latency breakdowns).
- Cons: Requires trust boundary work (you provide certs or allow us to manage certs stored in your KMS).
- Ops: We recommend customer-provided certs stored in KMS with cross-account access roles or short-lived certs issued from your internal PKI.

Option C — Hybrid: Customer terminates externally but delegate a private stub zone and short-lived certs for internal services
- Flow: Client -> Customer LB (terminates) -> internal -> Redwood endpoints with short-lived certs for service-to-service auth
- Pros: Best of both: you control external keys, Redwood manages internal cert lifecycle to reduce ops burden.
- Cons: More moving parts to coordinate (automation for CSR signing/rotation).

Recommended for PHI: Option A (TLS passthrough) for initial compliance signoff, with a roadmap to Option C for improved operations after SOC2 attestation. If you are comfortable delegating cert issuance to automation under strict IAM roles, Option B is viable but requires additional legal/controls mapping.

Minimal DNS / network steps (high-level):
- Create a private hosted zone in your VPC for *.redwood-prod.priv.healthtech.internal (or similar).
- Either CNAME or ALIAS from your internal FQDN -> Redwood private endpoint FQDN we provide.
- Ensure route tables and NACLs allow outbound connections from your LB to Redwood private endpoint IPs (we’ll share CIDR ranges).
- Optionally create a stub zone delegation to let your DNS servers resolve our internal endpoints directly.

Cert rotation and audit model (summary):
- If you manage certs: rotate per your policy, provide new certs to LB or upload to KMS; Redwood will perform connectivity checks and report results.
- If Redwood manages: we can use short-lived certs with CSR signed by your CA or use cross-account KMS to store private keys; we emit rotation events to your audit topic (CloudWatch/EventBridge) with runbook links.

Next steps I suggest:
1) Tell us which option you prefer for the compliance review (A/B/C).
2) If A, share LB hostname + NAT/VPC egress rules and we’ll validate connectivity.
3) If B or C, share your CSR policy and a sandbox KMS role we can use for a sample rotation.

I’m looping in Marissa and Karthik for SRE/security nuances; Mina can help with the cert automation flow. Happy to schedule a focused 30m to walk through the SOW changes.

—Connor
Connor O'Brien
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
From: marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: connor_obrien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>
Cc: karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, mina_haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.ai>, Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@healthtech.io>
Date: 2026-09-01T08:20:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Private deployment TLS — where to terminate certs?

Adding an operational checklist and a recommended responsibilities matrix for the three options — aim is to make compliance reviewers see clear ownership. I kept the wording intentional for audit docs.

Operational checklist (deliverables we can own vs you own):
- Inventory FQDNs and intended audience (client-facing vs internal): YOURS
- Private DNS delegation: CUSTOMER (create private hosted zone; optionally delegate stub to Redwood)
- LB termination certs: CUSTOMER (Option A/C) or CUSTOMER-provided + RW-managed rotation (Option B)
- KMS storage for cert keys: CUSTOMER (preferred) with cross-account role for RW test-only access; RW will not persist keys outside your KMS
- CSR & short-lived cert automation: RW can run CSR -> you sign (recommended) or sign via your internal CA on our request
- Rotation cadence: default 30 days for short-lived certs; 90 days for long-lived customer certs (configurable)

Action items for validation/testing:
1) Provide a sample internal FQDN we can resolve from a test instance.
2) Provide a sandbox KMS role ARN and KMS policy that allows GenerateDataKey and DescribeKey (we’ll scope to a single ARN).
3) Share your egress CIDR whitelist (or allowlist the Redwood private edge IPs).
4) Run an end-to-end smoke test where your LB routes to our endpoint and we validate chain, OCSP stapling (if applicable), and rotation events.

Risk notes for auditors (short):
- If customer keys remain in your KMS and you terminate TLS inside your VPC, there is no cryptographic material in Redwood-managed systems — highest control model.
- If Redwood manages certs, ensure IAM/roles are strictly scoped and rotation events are routed to your SIEM; we can emit signed rotation attestations.

Proposed timeline if we get sandbox access this week:
- Day 0–3: DNS and LB validation + sandbox KMS policy review
- Day 4–10: Implement automated CSR flow and initial rotation in staging
- Day 11–14: Smoke tests and compliance evidence collection (rotation logs, signed attestations)

Please confirm if we should treat this as an escalation (accelerate SLA) for the compliance review. If you confirm Option A today we can focus on immediate validation.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Head of Security Solutions, Redwood Inference

Thanks — that level of detail is perfect. For the immediate compliance review we’ll go with Option A (TLS passthrough to our LB). Two quick clarifications before we schedule the validation call:
1) Can Redwood still perform health checks on the runtime if we terminate (we can allow a dedicated health probe path)?
2) Will Redwood accept mutual-TLS client certs from our internal services for inter-service auth if we later move to Option C?

We can provide the sandbox KMS role ARN and a sample FQDN tomorrow. Targeting the compliance packet on 09/06, so the timeline you proposed looks OK. Please send a calendar invite for a 30-minute validation call for 09/04.

—Alex
